title: Slipped Disc and Sciatica: How Long Does It Take to Heal, and Do I Need Surgery?
metaDescription: Slipped disc with leg pain? Most sciatica settles without surgery. How long recovery takes, what helps, and the red flags that need urgent care.
intro: Back pain that shoots down one leg, often after lifting, sitting for hours or a bad night's sleep, sends many people straight to a scan and then to the internet. The word 'slipped disc' on an MRI report sounds alarming, and the next question is almost always: will this need an operation? For most people the honest answer is no. A smaller group, with specific warning signs or pain that refuses to settle, genuinely does better with surgery.

sections.heading: What is a slipped disc, and why does it cause leg pain?
sections.body: A 'slipped' disc (PIVD, or herniated disc) means the soft centre of a spinal disc has pushed through its outer layer and is pressing on a nearby nerve root. That nerve pain travels down the leg, and doctors call it sciatica. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons describes sciatica as nerve pain rather than a diagnosis in itself, usually from a herniated disc or spinal stenosis. Typical features are sharp, shooting pain from the buttock down the back of one leg, sometimes with numbness, tingling or weakness.

sections.heading: How long does a slipped disc with sciatica take to get better?
sections.body: Most people improve without surgery, usually over weeks to a few months. OrthoInfo (AAOS) states that roughly 80 to 90 percent of people with sciatica get better over time without an operation, typically within several weeks when a herniated disc is the cause, and that most patients are free of symptoms by 3 to 4 months. That is an average. Some settle in days, others take longer, and a minority do not settle at all. A scan helps once a decision about treatment is on the table, but it rarely changes what you do in the first weeks, because most herniated discs behave well with time.

sections.heading: What treatment helps while I wait?
sections.body: Staying gently active, rather than resting in bed, along with physiotherapy and short-term anti-inflammatory pain relief, is the usual first step. OrthoInfo lists rest, anti-inflammatory tablets, physical therapy and epidural steroid injections as options, and notes that these relieve symptoms while the body heals the disc; they do not repair it. Be cautious about nerve-pain tablets: NICE guidance in the UK advises against gabapentinoids and oral steroids for most people with sciatica because harms outweigh benefits.
bullets: Keep walking and moving within what pain allows; avoid prolonged bed rest.
A physiotherapist can guide graded exercise and posture for sitting and lifting.
Anti-inflammatory tablets help some people but have side effects (stomach, kidney, blood pressure), so check with a doctor before using them for more than a few days.
An epidural steroid injection is an option for severe leg pain that is not settling, as a way to ease symptoms while the disc recovers.

sections.heading: When do I actually need surgery for a slipped disc?
sections.body: Surgery is reasonable when disabling leg pain persists after about three months of proper non-surgical treatment, or sooner when there is muscle weakness, difficulty walking, or bladder or bowel changes. OrthoInfo says surgery is typically recommended only after a period of non-surgical treatment has failed, or for people with those more serious features. The scan must also match the symptoms: a disc bulge on MRI with no matching leg pain is not by itself a reason to operate.

sections.heading: Does earlier surgery give a better result?
sections.body: Earlier surgery tends to relieve leg pain faster, but the long-term outcome looks similar. In a Dutch randomised trial of 283 people with sciatica, early microdiscectomy gave faster relief than continued conservative care, yet outcomes were similar by one year and did not change in the second year. So for someone coping reasonably, waiting is a safe choice. For someone in severe pain who cannot work or sleep, choosing earlier surgery to shorten the pain is a legitimate decision, taken with eyes open.

sections.heading: If I do need surgery, what does a microdiscectomy involve?
sections.body: A microdiscectomy is a keyhole-sized operation that removes the piece of disc pressing on the nerve, and most people go home within 24 to 48 hours. As published on this site's spine page, walking starts the same day, light activity resumes within one to two weeks, and desk work is typically possible at two to four weeks, followed by physiotherapy to strengthen the core. Your own timeline depends on your job, the level of the disc and how long the nerve was compressed. Leg pain usually eases first; numbness or weakness can take longer to recover.

sections.heading: Which symptoms mean I should get seen urgently?
sections.body: Loss of bladder or bowel control, numbness around the groin or inner thighs, or a leg that is rapidly becoming weak needs same-day assessment. OrthoInfo calls loss of bladder or bowel control, although extremely rare, a sign of cauda equina syndrome, a medical emergency. Do not wait for a scheduled appointment; go to an emergency department or a spine surgeon immediately. Progressive foot weakness, such as a foot that begins to drag, also deserves prompt review rather than waiting out the usual three months.

faqs.q: Can a slipped disc heal on its own without surgery?
faqs.a: Yes, in most people. OrthoInfo states that roughly 80 to 90 percent of people with sciatica improve over time without surgery, typically within several weeks when a herniated disc is the cause, and most are free of symptoms by 3 to 4 months.

faqs.q: How long should I wait before considering surgery for sciatica?
faqs.a: Surgery is usually considered if disabling leg pain persists after about three months of non-surgical treatment. Earlier assessment is appropriate if you develop leg weakness, difficulty walking, or any bladder or bowel change.

faqs.q: My MRI shows a disc bulge. Does that mean I need an operation?
faqs.a: No. Surgery is decided by your symptoms and examination, with the scan as supporting evidence. Many people have disc bulges on MRI without symptoms, so imaging alone is not a reason to operate.

faqs.q: Is walking good or bad for a slipped disc?
faqs.a: Staying gently active is generally better than prolonged bed rest, and OrthoInfo lists continued movement as part of non-surgical care. Stop or modify any activity that sharply worsens leg pain, and see a doctor if weakness or numbness is increasing.

faqs.q: Can a slipped disc come back after surgery?
faqs.a: It can. OrthoInfo notes up to a 20 to 25 percent chance of a disc herniating again in your lifetime after a herniated disc, and that microdiscectomy results are generally very good. Core strengthening and sensible lifting habits are part of lowering that risk.
